_capture.artefact: Tier 0 payload-equality fixture — B8a account & profile
_capture.provenance: SYNTHETIC — and, like B9b's chat fixture, this one could not be a recording even in principle: these are REQUEST bodies, and obtaining a real one means writing to a live citizen's profile, preferences or PASSWORD on staging, which the slot 16-47 capture session explicitly refused ('This capture performed ZERO writes to the account', manifest-authenticated.md). B2-AC-36's 'real recorded staging payloads' standard is therefore reported NOT EVALUATED with that reason and never PASS. expected_body is DERIVED, not recorded: each one is what AccountPage.tsx:212-215 / :252-256 / :280 over client.ts's JSON.stringify produces for that input, computed by applying the source's own transform rather than transcribed by eye. NO REAL CITIZEN DATA: every name, email, address, UIN and password below is invented for this file (B8-AC-35). The passwords are not credentials for any system.
_capture.credential: none — no host was contacted to build this file, and no password here is or has ever been a real one
_capture.why_asymmetric: The one real transform in B8a is handleSaveProfile's dirty-field diff, and its three branches are NOT symmetric: `name` is guarded by truthiness AND difference (AccountPage.tsx:213), while `email` and `address` are guarded by difference alone (:214, :215). So clearing the name sends NOTHING for it, and clearing the email sends `email: ""`. A fixture set in which every case changes all three fields passes for EVERY plausible implementation, including the tidy one-loop rewrite a careful developer reaches for first. The cases below are chosen so the two provably differ, and tier0_account_payload_test.dart asserts the INEQUALITY against that naive implementation as well as the equality against the real one: a fixture that stopped discriminating fails the test rather than passing it. FACTORY-RULES' Capability Rule, applied to a five-line transform (B8-AC-31).
_capture.why_whole_object: PUT /me/preferences is a PUT, not a PATCH (endpoints.ts:123), and updatePrefs merges the nested `notifications` object SEPARATELY from the outer one (AccountPage.tsx:255). So toggling one switch transmits all five fields. A shallow-spread port silently resets the two untouched booleans server-side and the UI still looks correct, because it refetches. The prefs_* cases below assert the whole object and the INEQUALITY against a shallow-spread implementation (B8-AC-33).
_capture.key_order: expected_body is a STRING, not an object, because key order is part of the claim. Dart Map literals preserve insertion order and jsonEncode respects it, so asserting the encoded string gates the ORDER as well as the names and values (F0 § 6.2.3, followed by B9b).

cases.note: THE DISCRIMINATING CASE. The citizen empties the name field and edits the email. `name` is falsy after trim, so :213's truthiness guard omits it entirely; `email` differs, so :214 includes it. The naive symmetric implementation sends `name: ""` and is a DIFFERENT REQUEST — asserted as an inequality.

The sharpest form of the same asymmetry: clearing ONLY the name produces an EMPTY body, so the source issues NO REQUEST AT ALL and shows `nothingChanged` (:216-219). The naive implementation issues a PATCH that blanks the citizen's name. B8-AC-31 case (i) + (iv) at once.
B8-AC-31 case (ii). `email` is guarded by difference ALONE, so an empty email IS transmitted — the opposite disposition from `name`, in the same function, three lines apart.
B8-AC-31 case (iii) — exactly one key. A port that sent the whole form would send three.
B8-AC-31 case (iv). Every field equals the account's, so the body is empty and NO request is issued. The BLoC test asserts the zero invocation count; this asserts the body it would have sent.

The comparison is on the TRIMMED value (`form.name.trim() !== account.name`), so padding a field with spaces is not an edit. A port that compared the raw value would issue a PATCH for a citizen who touched nothing.

The CONTROL that proves nothing on its own: with all three fields edited, the real implementation and the naive one agree exactly. Kept because it is the reason the cases above exist — a fixture set made only of this shape would report PASS for a port that got `name` wrong.

A Lao name, so the trim/compare path is exercised on non-ASCII. `String.prototype.trim` and Dart's `String.trim` both strip Unicode whitespace, and neither touches the combining marks inside the name — but B9b's subject-slice defect is the reason this project no longer assumes an ASCII fixture covers Lao.
